lines: Our primary analysis uses a single environment (ScienceWorld, 11 of 30 task types) with one backbone (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct); generalization requires further validation. The $-100$ death penalty amplifies DAF; environments with softer penalties would exhibit lower DAF values (Appendix~\ref{app:penalty}). The 19 excluded task types (63\%) lack routing signal because both strategies typically time out within 30 steps; increasing the step budget could surface non-death-dominated signal that our current setup does not capture. Cross-environment analyses on MATH and ALFWorld (\S\ref{sec:cross-env}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}) provide preliminary supporting evidence but do not conclusively establish generalization. A Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct cross-model replication (11 task types, $N{=}220$; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}) shows death dominance replicates with direction consistency 10/10 while vulnerability magnitude varies ($+30.0$~pp vs.\ Qwen $+26.5$~pp), though both models are in the 7--8B parameter range; Qwen2.5-72B ($10{\times}$ scale) reduces death rate but does not eliminate death dominance (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}); validation beyond 72B remains future work. Our quantitative results (DAF $= 90.4\%$, label fractions) are specific to ScienceWorld; the framework's generality claim is methodological (the diagnostic procedure applies to any environment with asymmetric fatal outcomes), not empirical (the specific percentages may differ across environments).
\paragraph{Methodological constraints.}

-Our internal-reasoning baseline uses single-pass ReAct~\citep{react-2023}. Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023} reduces death rate from 42.9\% to 31.4\% (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}), but more aggressive self-correction or Tree-of-Thought backtracking~\citep{tot-2023} may further reduce internal death rates. Episode-level labels assign a single routing preference to entire episodes, which may be suboptimal for individual steps (particularly those preceding death events). However, only 0.3\% of training steps exhibit directional conflict with episode labels (7/2,040); the dominant issue is not mislabeling but the 97.4\% step-level tie rate, which leaves the router with almost no per-step signal to learn from. Training on pure-strategy trajectories also introduces distribution shift at deployment~\citep{dagger-2011}. More broadly, projecting episode-level labels onto 10--50 sequential steps with path-dependent state introduces compounding error: early routing decisions alter the state trajectory, potentially invalidating later labels derived from the episode outcome.

\paragraph{Statistical limitations.}

Episodes within the same task type are not fully independent because they share environment dynamics, though they use different random seeds. lines: \subsection{Router Training as Diagnostic Probe}
\label{sec:router-diagnostic}

-We probe whether counterfactual labels can train a step-level router as a diagnostic of label informativeness. The oracle margin (2.89 points) caps routing upside; at step level, of 2{,}040 training steps only 0.3\% exhibit strict directional conflict (step-level oracle opposite to episode label); the remaining non-tie steps are episode labels applied where neither strategy has a step-level advantage (60.3\% pre-event neutral), a granularity mismatch rather than label error, leaving minimal signal for the router to exploit. An implicit router (Qwen3, LoRA; Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}) trained at three scales (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B) with 4-seed configurations shows flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\%$, within seed variance). At episode level, only 4B exceeds always-deterministic ($59.0 \pm 1.9\%$, $p < 0.005$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}); 0.6B and 1.7B remain at or below chance. The multi-step nature of routing (10--50 actions with compounding state uncertainty) creates inherent label noise between step-level decisions and episode-level outcomes. Training and validation use episode-level splits (Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}), ensuring no within-episode information leakage.

**(a) Routing 文献 prior assumptions**：
"Existing routing work (Toolformer, CogRouter, ART, When2Tool, RouteLLM) implicitly assumes diverse routing signals—capability matching, efficiency, task complexity. No prior work has quantified signal composition. Our finding that a single mechanism (death avoidance) accounts for 78.9% of routing labels contradicts this implicit diversity assumption."

**(b) Intervention resistance non-predictability**：
"From the setup alone (P=100, internal DR=42.9%), one might predict that scaling (72B), self-correction (Reflexion), or action filtering would substantially reduce death vulnerability. Instead, all four intervention axes fail to eliminate death dominance: 72B DAF=92.4%, Reflexion DAF>100% (Δ_nd=-0.47, meaning self-correction improves non-death performance while death dominance remains intact), action filtering reduces DR to 29% but ≥12pp residual gap persists. This resistance pattern is non-obvious from the experimental setup."

- C1: "We propose an episode-level counterfactual diagnostic framework that overcomes per-step oracle degeneracy (97.4% tie rate) in sparse-reward environments, enabling signal decomposition at the episode level."

**Abstract narrative**：framework → application → finding → validation → implication。Concept-first, numbers-second。
